nodes.summary: Let $a$, $b$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $0 < b < a$, $a$ and $b$ coprime, and $n \ge 2$, and suppose that $(a, b, n)$ is not a Bang–Zsigmondy exceptional case: neither $(a, b, n) = (2, 1, 6)$, nor $n = 2$ with $a + b$ a power of two. Then $a^n - b^n$ has a primitive prime divisor, that is, a prime $p$ that divides $a^n - b^n$ and divides no $a^m - b^m$ with $1 \le m < n$.
nodes.title: Zsigmondy's theorem

nodes.summary: A triple $(a, b, n)$ of natural numbers is a Bang–Zsigmondy exceptional case when either $(a, b, n) = (2, 1, 6)$, or $n = 2$ and $a + b = 2^k$ for some natural number $k$.
nodes.title: Exceptional cases of Zsigmondy's theorem
